stories.title: Energy prices rise by 19% in a year -report
stories.preview: The Retail Prices Indices and Household Costs Indices inflation statistics have been published.
stories.summary: The Retail Prices Indices and Household Costs Indices inflation statistics have been published.
stories.whyItMatters: Persistent inflation can keep bond yields higher and reduce the diversification benefit of nominal bonds during supply shocks. The practical response is usually broad diversification and an intentional duration mix, not a reaction to one data point.

stories.title: New U.S. tariffs extend the inflation-and-growth trade-off
stories.preview: Replacement tariffs of 10% to 12.5% now cover dozens of U.S. trading partners. The bigger issue is not one day’s market reaction, but a longer period of higher import costs and policy uncertainty.
stories.summary: The United States replaced its temporary 10% tariff with country-specific levies ranging from 10% to 12.5%, effective 24 July. The rates are not dramatically above the temporary regime and include carve-outs, but they make a higher tariff baseline more persistent. Yale’s Budget Lab estimated the average U.S. tariff rate at about 11% and an eventual household cost of roughly $1,100. Tariffs can raise selected goods prices, reduce firms’ willingness to invest and complicate central-bank decisions—especially while energy prices are also elevated. The economic effect will depend on exemptions, exchange rates, supply-chain changes and how much of the cost businesses absorb rather than pass on.
stories.whyItMatters: For a diversified investor, this is a reason to keep both inflation and slower-growth outcomes in the plan. Geographic diversification, inflation-sensitive assets and a deliberate mix of short- and longer-duration bonds matter more than guessing which tariff headline comes next.

stories.title: Forecasters cut euro-area growth while inflation stays above target
stories.preview: ECB-survey respondents now expect only 0.6% euro-area growth in 2026, alongside 2.7% inflation. That mix argues for patience rather than a simple ‘rates down, bonds up’ narrative.
stories.summary: The ECB’s quarterly survey of professional forecasters cut expected euro-area growth for 2026 by 0.4 percentage points to 0.6%, and trimmed 2027 growth to 1.2%. Headline inflation expectations stayed at 2.7% for 2026 and rose slightly to 2.2% for 2027; longer-run inflation expectations remained anchored at 2.0%. Respondents expect most indirect effects of the Middle East war to be concentrated in 2026, with inflation risks tilted upward this year. Forecasts are not facts, but the combination of weak growth and sticky near-term inflation shows why the ECB has limited room for quick, uncomplicated easing.
stories.whyItMatters: For long-horizon allocation, slower growth supports the defensive role of high-quality bonds, while sticky inflation limits how much duration to add based on growth alone. Broad global equity exposure also reduces dependence on one region’s weak cycle.

stories.title: Oil above $100 turns geopolitics back into an inflation problem
stories.preview: Brent crude moved back above $100 as threats spread to a second major Middle Eastern shipping route. The durable issue is a renewed supply shock that can lift inflation while weakening growth.
stories.summary: Brent crude rose back above $100 a barrel after Houthi forces claimed attacks on Saudi tankers and threatened the Red Sea route, adding a second chokepoint to disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. Oil had traded below $70 before the U.S. war with Iran, so the change is large enough to affect fuel, freight and production costs. U.S. gasoline moved above $4 a gallon, while diesel and jet-fuel costs were also rising. The path remains highly uncertain: spare capacity, alternative routes and any de-escalation could reverse prices, but prolonged disruption would feed into inflation and household purchasing power across many economies.
stories.whyItMatters: Oil shocks can hurt both stocks and nominal bonds by slowing growth while lifting inflation. That is precisely why a resilient allocation mixes growth assets with high-quality bonds of different maturities and, where appropriate, inflation-sensitive exposure rather than relying on one hedge for every downturn.

stories.title: ECB pauses at 2.25% while the energy shock works through inflation
stories.preview: The ECB left rates unchanged after June’s increase. Energy prices are now the key uncertainty: high enough to threaten inflation, but also capable of weakening growth.
stories.summary: The European Central Bank kept its deposit rate at 2.25%, the main refinancing rate at 2.40% and the marginal lending rate at 2.65%. It said energy prices remain well above their pre-conflict level and that the full inflationary effect of the Middle East shock has not yet appeared. The ECB is watching for indirect effects as higher energy costs pass into other prices and wages, while avoiding a fixed promise about its next move. This is a classic supply-shock problem: tighter policy can restrain inflation expectations, but it cannot produce more energy and may further slow an already soft economy.
stories.whyItMatters: European bond yields may stay sensitive to energy and inflation data even if growth is weak. The long-term lesson is to avoid treating bonds as one uniform bucket: cash, short-duration bonds, long-duration government bonds and inflation-linked bonds serve different roles.

stories.title: Japan’s growth ambitions meet a less forgiving bond market
stories.preview: Japan’s government wants to accelerate investment in strategic industries, but rising government-bond yields show that financing conditions can no longer be taken for granted. The tension matters well beyond Japan because its bond market is one of the world’s largest.
stories.summary: Japan’s new economic blueprint emphasises state-backed investment in growth industries, while investors are increasingly focused on inflation and the fiscal cost of new commitments. Japanese government-bond yields have risen as the Bank of Japan reduces extraordinary support and the market asks for more compensation to hold long-dated debt. Higher domestic yields can change the incentives of Japanese institutions that own large amounts of overseas bonds: some foreign assets become less attractive once currency hedging is included. The result is a structural adjustment, not merely a one-day sell-off, and it may unfold unevenly as policy and inflation expectations change.
stories.whyItMatters: This is a reminder that duration risk exists even in historically low-yield markets. A globally diversified bond allocation should account for currency hedging, maturity and issuer quality rather than assuming every sovereign bond market will behave like U.S. Treasuries.
